This is the first of a two-part series where we share our findings and learning points from Project Toaster, an OSINT-based project using agentic AI to monitor and predict the 2026 Johor State Election (JSE). Part 1 covers what we set out to do, how we designed the experiment, and what we built. Part 2 will be the post-mortem.

01 · The OG problemHow it all started

What if one human had to cover a fast-paced, noisy election all alone, but could summon an army of agents to help?

That was the genesis of Project Toaster, a harebrained experiment to see if we could use agents to monitor and make sense of fast-moving, dynamic situations awash with news and social media data. Elections are the textbook case: a fixed deadline, a flood of posts and articles in several languages, and a scoreboard at the end that tells you whether you read the room right. In the spirit of build fast, try small and fail cheaply, the Johor State Election of 11 July 2026 was the guinea pig of choice.

📅
It was happening soon enough
Almost two months from the day Toaster was commissioned. Long enough to build something, short enough to force choices.
🧭
We knew the theatre
We had Malaysia expertise on the team to design the experiment, formulate the hypotheses, and decide on sensible data metrics for the test.
🌊
It was the right shape of problem
A fast-moving, dynamic, OSINT-heavy event, as most elections are. If agents could not help here, they were unlikely to help anywhere.

02 · Project creepWhat really happened

Also known as: what happens when you give an analyst and a data scientist free rein.

What started as a little single-slice toaster build very quickly morphed into one that toasted four slices of bread at once, with a little button for those who wanted their toast just a little more toasty.

Monitorthe OG slice
Predictseats, twice a day
Briefthe Daily Toast
Dashboardone screen for all of it
manual override

The project grew into one to build agents that could (1) monitor the election, (2) predict the outcome, and (3) push out a twice-daily situation report of around 400 words on the state of play, all served through a dashboard that let an analyst see the evidence, the forecast and the reasoning in one place. We were catering to different consumer demands while trying to remain true to the OG plot: use agents to monitor and track an election. The "little button" was a set of manual override dials, so that a human who disagreed with the agents could nudge the forecast and see what changed.

03 · Design, then buildHow we came up with the blueprints

We adopted a two-part approach. First, design the toaster: work out the problem, the hypotheses, and the indicators that would tell us whether the hypotheses were holding. Only then build the machine: find the data and build the components that track those indicators.

1Design the toaster

Identify the problem
Formulate the hypotheses
Agree on appropriate indicators

2Build the machine

Obtain the necessary data sources
Build the components to track the indicators
Put it all on one dashboard

Once the toaster had been designed, the analyst and the data scientist sat down to argue about the data: could we even get it, how robust was it, and what would a dashboard built on it actually look like. That conversation shaped everything that followed, so we describe it in some detail in the Build sections.

04 · DesignThe question, the yardstick, and the hypotheses

Identifying the question

Just like all good papers, Toaster started with a list of questions and hypotheses that we wanted to test.

Placeholder · main questions (WIP in outline)

Insert the main questions the project set out to answer. The outline marks this as "insert later".

But such questions were too complex for a little machine to answer, and really belonged to big-brained human analysts with access to far more information than Toaster would ever see. We had to break them down into a question that data could answer directly.

The big questionsWhat the analysts actually want to know about Johor, its parties and its voters. (See placeholder above.)
What a machine can be tested onSomething with a number attached and a scoreboard at the end.
The question we gave ToasterWhich coalition will win the JSE, and by how many seats?

Defining what success would look like

±5%
Primary yardstick: predict the JSE result within a 5% margin of error. Blunt, but easy to score.
Less to read
Secondary yardstick: help people monitor the JSE more efficiently by doing a first cut of the data, so humans process less raw material.

Oh how far we had strayed from the OG objective. The monitoring goal had become the secondary measure.

Formulating hypotheses and frameworks

We used long-existing frameworks and assumptions, building on what we knew about Johor's quirks and trying to explicitly tease out the assumptions that had become second nature. It took time. A lot of it. Even in partnership with the most expensive frontier models we could throw money at (hello, Claude Opus 4.8 Max). Writing down what you think you know turns out to be much slower than knowing it.

Assumptions

The core assumption
★Whoever is able to meet voter demand will win the most seats. The whole framework is built around this.
How the parties would play it
01BN would use the same playbook it had used for every by-election since 2022: concentrate all its resources on one campaign, focus on local issues, keep its distance from the federal government, hype how Johor has benefited from the BN state government, tap the pull of the royals, trot out Menteri Besar Onn Hafiz as the poster boy, and reduce Zahid's presence.
02Zahid was still toxic, and his presence would hurt BN's chances at the ballot box.
03Hadi's presence in Johor would indicate that PAS was making a push into the state.
04DAP's campaign would focus on federal projects like the RTS Link to try to maximise Chinese turnout.
05Bersama would split the PH vote.
06Syed Saddiq would retain Puteri Wangsa because he is personally popular.
07Incumbents have an advantage in their seats.
How the voters would behave
08The royals have some ability to swing the Malay vote, but we would not be able to quantify the effect.
09MCA has lost the Chinese vote. The Chinese will vote DAP if they bother to turn up.
10Low turnout benefits BN; high turnout (which in practice means Chinese turnout) does not, and is good for PH. This is based on the 2022 JSE, where low overall turnout, especially among Chinese voters, benefited BN.
11PN supporters will vote BN in seats where PN is not running, and PN where it is.
12The Chinese, especially those working in Singapore, are unlikely to return to vote.
What the data could tell us
13Sentiment analysis from news reporting, leader visits, likes and comments will help predict seat winners.

Framework

Our framework was a simple equation based on the core assumption: the coalition best able to meet voter demands would win. In short, voter demand + parties' ability to supply = votes. Tap any item to see how we planned to measure it.

We also acknowledged that the framework would never fully cover everything that determines turnout, which depends on many factors, including the weather on the day itself.

05 · BuildThree interfaces for covering an election

When we thought about how the machine would actually be used, three interfaces fell out, each with a different job for the AI. Monitoring is where AI extracts information. Predicting is where it makes assessments. Updating is where it summarises. Keeping the three jobs separate mattered more than we expected, because it let us choose a different level of trust in the AI for each.

Interface 1

Monitoring

What it doesTracks a short list of indicators we hypothesised would show where the election was heading.
What the AI doesExtracts information: reads posts, comments and articles and turns them into labelled, structured rows.
IndicatorsVoter preference by race · voter sentiment from news comments · campaign activity · key leader presence in Johor · royal signals · foreign (Singapore) mentions.
Interface 2

Predicting

What it doesTurns the indicators into a seat-by-seat forecast through a statistical prediction engine.
What the AI doesMakes assessments: judges which way each indicator is pointing, and how strongly, to set the engine's inputs.
Inputs it setsOpposition Malay voters' PH-vs-PN lean (rural and urban) · turnout scenario (overall and the Malay–Chinese gap) · change in Malay and Chinese support for BN versus 2022 · seat-specific nudges.
Interface 3

Updating

What it doesSends a regular update, up to twice a day, with a news round-up and the latest forecast.
What the AI doesSummarises: writes a short narrative from the numbers the engine produced and the evidence that moved them.
OutputThe Daily Toast: about 400 words, morning and evening.

06 · BuildData sources, and how we weighted them

We obtained our list of candidate data sources from an extensive literature review, courtesy of Claude, and cross-referenced it against the sources we already used. The analyst and the data scientist then went through it together and asked two questions of every source: is it feasible to get in the time we have, and how much should it count given the question we are trying to answer? The constraint was brutal in a good way. We had weeks, not months, to find data and build pipelines, so anything that needed a long negotiation or a fragile scraper was out.

How we graded them

We sorted indicators into four broad baskets, graded A to D, on how well they have historically correlated with election results and how reliably they can be measured.

GradeRubric definitionWhat that means, and how the indicator is treated
AStrong diagnostic power, correlation at or above 0.7. Measurement validated and stable over time.Either a vote that has already happened, or opinion sampled by an instrument with a documented method. Allowed to drive the forecast on its own.
BModerate diagnostic power, correlation between 0.4 and 0.7. Some measurement concern or volatility.Sound in principle, but each has a known direction of error: approval is flattered by politeness, campaign activity is both cause and effect.
CWeak but real, correlation between 0.2 and 0.4. Substantial measurement or noise problems.Carries genuine information, but only after heavy processing, and never enough to overturn anything above it. Capped so it cannot rise.
DUnclear or negative diagnostic value in the Malaysian context.Either unavailable in practice, or so distorted that assuming nothing beats believing it. Listed with reasons, then ignored.

The rubric grades on correlation with the eventual result: 1.0 would be perfect lockstep, 0 would be no relationship at all.

07 · BuildMonitoring

We explored new types of data, and new ways of using data we already had, to get more diagnostic indicators. Six made it into the live system. What follows is the list, how each one was measured, and the thinking behind it.

IndicatorMethodologyThe thinking
Voter preference by raceOpinion poll data from reputable pollsters, found by an agent that ran a web search every day for new polls and extracted the support levels by ethnic group.The only measured input. Everything else is a proxy.
Voter sentiment from news commentsSentiment of public comments left under mainstream media's Facebook posts on politics, labelled by target (BN, PH, PN, the Johor government, the federal government) and language (Malay, Chinese, English).Comments are where readers argue back. The caveat: we may be over-weighting a vocal minority.
Campaign activityTrack campaign activity through the parties' own social media posts about ceramahs and walkabouts.Assumes parties post about their campaign efforts on their official accounts. They do, relentlessly.
Key leader presence in JohorTrack leaders' presence using their own social media posts: is this leader physically campaigning in Johor today?We hypothesised an inverted U: more leader activity signals a seat's importance, up to a point; beyond it, a flurry of visits signals a lack of confidence in winning.
Royal signalsThe royal household's social media posts, plus news articles reporting royal statements, read for explicit and coded leans.The royals are constitutionally non-partisan, so explicit endorsements are rare. Coded signals are not.
Foreign mentionsKeyword filtering of news articles and posts to capture Malaysian politicians talking about Singapore during the campaign, then a second pass to classify who said it and to whom they were appealing.Shown for context on the dashboard and in the briefing. It does not feed the forecast.
A note on the comment-sentiment indicator. Technically it is our version of social-media sentiment analysis, which we otherwise rejected (see below). The difference is scope: instead of trying to score the whole of Malaysian social media, we scored only the replies under mainstream outlets' political posts, and we read the result as relative reception among an engaged, biased sample, never as vote share.

What the monitoring views looked like

Each indicator got its own panel on the Monitoring side of the dashboard. Click any image to enlarge.

Data we explored and rejected

We considered the following sources of data and rejected them for various reasons. Some of these are the most interesting part of the story, because they are where the theatre knowledge earned its keep.

Type of dataWhy we considered itWhy we rejected it
Prediction markets such as PolymarketHarness the wisdom of the local crowd, who might have a better sense of ground sentiment towards the parties.Hard to obtain from online sources. There was exactly one Polymarket bet on the JSE and it was thinly traded (the price barely moved).
Raw social media postsSentiment analysis of social media would be a natural way to gauge mood, with so much campaigning happening online.Hard to determine causality and direction from sentiment analysis, which remains a greenfield area and is largely limited to crude positive / neutral / negative scoring. We kept a narrower version: comments under news posts.
Chinese press sentimentOne of the few places to learn what Chinese voters are thinking.Literature and our own reading suggest Chinese-press sentiment is not diagnostic of Chinese voter sentiment. Superseded by tracking Chinese-language comments left on political news posts.
WhatsApp and Telegram closed groupsA considerable amount of news spreads through closed groups, especially among voters over 60, who tend to swing between BN and PN.No access to closed groups. We also looked at news outlets' Telegram channels to track reactions, but the Malaysian channels we checked (Malaysiakini, FMT) had reactions turned off.
JAKIM's list of accredited preachersAn unexplored way of checking whether Johor-based preachers were endorsing candidates, as a proxy for the Malay religious vote and PAS's penetration of Johor.Hard to pin down which preachers are Johor-based even with the list, which may not be complete; many of Malaysia's religious influencers are not accredited; and tracking them down online and scraping their posts is technically expensive.
TikTok hashtagsGrowing TikTok use suggests hashtags could show which issues were gaining traction, especially among young voters.Difficulties getting the data.

Things we found but did not explore, for lack of time

YOLO v8
A family of single-stage object detectors that can estimate how many people are in a photo. Could turn small-scale ceramah turnouts into a proxy for eventual voter turnout.
Specialised crowd-counting CNNs
Count dense crowds where bodies overlap and detection-based methods miss heads, by regressing a density map over the image. Could do the same for large ceramahs.

08 · BuildPredicting

AI can think through a problem and make judgements, but it struggles with complex computation unless it has tools. A model might hallucinate on a tough mental sum, yet its odds of getting the right answer are far better when you hand it a calculator. Since election outcomes can be analysed and represented by statistical modelling, an election prediction should not come from gut feel, meaning a number an LLM throws out. It should come from a model whose assumptions you can see.

Step one: build a prediction engine

To ground the prediction in a statistical model, we combined past election results with theatre knowledge about how Malaysians tend to vote, namely along racial and rural-versus-urban lines. The result is what we called the first-principles engine. It is not machine learning. It is the arithmetic an analyst would do by hand for one seat, run consistently across all 56.

A seat's BN share = how each community votes × who actually turns out, plus the seat's own local history.The whole model in one line. Everything else is bookkeeping.

Three ideas do the work. First, communities turn out at different rates, so the electorate that actually votes is a different mix from the one on the register: in 2022 a seat that was 50% Malay on the roll was roughly 59% Malay at the ballot box, because Malay turnout was 20 points higher than Chinese turnout. Second, within each community, support for BN is roughly uniform across the state, so two numbers (Malay support, Chinese support) explain most of the variation between seats. Third, whatever those two numbers do not explain about a seat (a popular incumbent, a local grudge, the Indian vote we could not model separately) is stubbornly persistent from one election to the next, so we carry it forward.

The engine then exposes six dials. Set them, and it re-computes all 56 seats: how much Malay and Chinese support for BN has shifted since 2022; overall turnout and the Malay–Chinese turnout gap; and how the non-BN Malay vote splits between PH and PN in rural and in urban seats. After nomination day we added contest awareness, so each seat is modelled on the parties actually standing there: PN absent in 23 seats, the PH splinter Bersama in 15, two incumbents who switched coalitions.

Two benefits came free with this approach. The assumptions behind any prediction are transparent: a disagreement about the forecast becomes an argument about a specific, inspectable input. And the engine doubles as a sensitivity-analysis tool: what set of inputs would it take for BN to lose its majority? You can find out by turning the dials.

⚙️ Under the hoodThe engine, stage by stage, and how it was backtested

The model is estimated in three stages of ordinary least squares, all without intercepts, on three elections held on identical seat boundaries (2013, 2018, 2022). Every parameter is interpretable.

Stage 1, who turns out. Seat turnout is the composition-weighted average of community turnout rates. This recovers implied statewide rates for Malay (TM), Chinese (TC) and Indian (TI) voters.

Turnout_s = T_M · Malay%_s + T_C · Chinese%_s + T_I · Indian%_s + ε_s

Stage 2, effective composition. Because communities turn out at different rates, each seat's effective (voting) composition differs from its registered one.

Malay_eff_s = (Malay%_s × T_M) / Turnout_s (and similarly for Chinese, Indian)

Stage 3, how they vote. BN vote share is regressed on effective Malay and Chinese composition only. Indian voters are deliberately excluded, so their contribution, alongside candidate quality and local factors, is absorbed into the seat residual. BC should therefore be read as a Chinese-plus-Indian combined rate.

BN%_s = B_M · Malay_eff_s + B_C · Chinese_eff_s + residual_s

Stage 4, forward prediction. The previous election's residuals are carried forward at full strength as seat fixed effects; per-seat turnout is derived from composition under the chosen turnout scenario, not assumed known.

BN_pred_s = (B_M + ΔMalay) · Malay_eff_next,s + (B_C + ΔChinese) · Chinese_eff_next,s + residual_prev,s
Parameter201320182022
BM · Malay BN support84.3%65.1%60.7%
BC · Chinese (+Indian) BN support19.9%10.0%12.8%
TM · Malay turnout88.5%85.1%66.2%
TC · Chinese turnout85.6%85.4%45.8%
TI · Indian turnout93.2%88.5%36.6%
In-sample RMSE6.3 pp6.7 pp9.8 pp

Two readings of that table matter. Malay BN support declined monotonically, 84% to 65% to 61%: BN's 2022 seat recovery (40 of 56) was not a support recovery but the product of the turnout gap and a split opposition. And the higher 2022 RMSE reflects genuinely larger idiosyncratic variance (PN competing seriously for the first time), not model deterioration.

Backtests. To predict year T from year T−1, the backtest supplies the year-T support and turnout rates as known (what polls and rolls could in principle provide) and bets only on the carried-forward residuals and the derived per-seat turnout. Two reference runs bracket each test: composition only (residuals zeroed) and an in-sample ceiling (true year-T residuals).

RunRMSEMAECorrect callsBN seats
2018 → 2022 (actual BN seats: 40)
Composition only8.86 pp7.03 pp48/5640
2018 residuals carried forward5.04 pp4.03 pp52/5640
In-sample ceiling2.77 pp1.98 pp54/5640
2013 → 2018 (actual BN seats: 19)
Composition only6.82 pp5.47 pp46/5621
2013 residuals carried forward4.71 pp3.81 pp52/5619
In-sample ceiling1.11 pp0.75 pp——

Two successful out-of-sample trials on maximally different elections, one where BN collapsed and one where it recovered, and the exact statewide BN seat count in both. The four wrong calls in 2022 (Bukit Kepong, Tangkak, Yong Peng, Parit Yaani) were all pre-flagged as marginal and offset two-for-two. Residual persistence across one cycle is strong (r = 0.74 for 2013→2018, 0.85 for 2018→2022) and decays over two (0.59), so residuals are carried forward one election only.

Known limitations, disclosed to every user of the dashboard.

  1. The backtest is a best case: true support and turnout rates were supplied. In live use they come from polls, and input error propagates roughly one-for-one into every seat of similar composition. Real forward error will exceed 5 pp.
  2. Support levels are weakly identified; the Malay–Chinese gap is not. Effective Malay and Chinese shares are near-complementary (r ≈ −0.95), so the data pins down the gap (~48 pp in 2022) far more tightly than the individual levels. Translating a poll number directly onto BM is less exact than the dials imply.
  3. Indian voters are not separately modelled.
  4. The opposition side is modelled coarsely: the engine is validated for BN performance, and PH-versus-PN outcomes rest on weaker footing.
  5. One state, two transitions, 56 seats. Parameters do not transfer elsewhere without refitting, and a boundary redelineation would break residual carry-forward.
  6. Residuals are a one-cycle asset; the baseline should always be the most recent election.

Defensible as a scenario tool and a device for spotting marginal seats. Not defensible as a point predictor of individual marginals, a poll-free forecast, or a PH-versus-PN model.

Step two: put AI agents in charge of the dials

With the engine in place, the AI's job became precise: turn the monitoring indicators into the engine's inputs. Five specialist agents each read one slice of the evidence, and a sixth component, a rules-based editor, combines their views into the six numbers and the per-seat nudges. We called the five the analysts.

Voter-preference poll arithmetic
An agent runs a daily web search for new opinion polls and extracts support levels by ethnic group. The shifts in Malay and Chinese BN support are then plain subtraction from the 2022 baselines. The only measured input, so it dominates when a fresh, relevant poll exists.
Voter-response judgment
Reads the comment-sentiment index and party-page engagement. Keeps two instruments separate: sentiment polarity may move the support deltas; engagement volume may only move turnout. Loud is not the same as persuaded. Owns four of the six numbers.
Campaign judgment
Reads per-seat campaign intensity against each seat's 2022 baseline. Activity shows a party is active in a seat, not that it is winning it; the hard call is whether heavy activity is persuasion or defence. Sole owner of the per-seat overrides.
Leader-interest judgment
Judges one thing: where the non-BN Malay vote is splitting between PH and PN, rural and urban separately, by reading where party leaders physically go in Johor.
Royal-signals drift formula
A formula over the royal feed. The model work happened earlier, when each royal post or article was read for its lean and salience.
The editor no AI
Combines everyone's signals into the final parameter set, the per-seat overrides, an overall confidence and the executive summary shown on the dashboard.
Code computes; the AI only classifies and judges direction.The one rule that kept the system honest.

The AI never does arithmetic, counts nothing and invents no percentage. A signal from an analyst is never a number. It is three judgements: a direction (BN stronger or weaker), a size band (small, moderate, large) and a confidence band (low, medium, high), with reasoning and citations attached. An analyst with nothing reliable to say abstains, and a silent analyst never dilutes the others. Ordinary code then turns the bands into numbers using fixed, published weights, so the same evidence always moves the dials by the same amount.

The pipeline, end to end

Every number on the dashboard is built by a chain of small, inspectable steps. Some are an AI model reading text; some are plain arithmetic. Tap any node for what it does.

🤖 Extraction
An AI model reads unstructured text and labels it, turning posts, comments and articles into clean structured rows. It reads; it does not weigh the race.
🧠 Judgment
An AI model reasons over already-aggregated data and emits an analytical signal: a direction, a strength and a confidence, with its reasoning and citations.
⚙️ Deterministic
Plain code, no AI. Counts, formulas and weighting. This is where labels become an index and a signal becomes a number on the dial.

Scroll the diagram sideways to see all seven stages.

Tap a node above.

Over the campaign the extraction models processed thousands of items a day. For scale: the final week alone held about 2,400 news items and 2,800 party posts in the feeds, and by polling day the sentiment index rested on roughly 114,000 labelled comments. The judgment agents, by contrast, ran only twice a day, and they never saw a raw comment. They saw the index.

⚙️ Under the hoodWho moves each dial, by how much, and the poll blend

Only certain analysts own each parameter, each with a fixed weight. Owners combine as a weighted average, never a sum, so agreement reinforces direction but can never exceed the strongest single owner. The band step is how far a small, moderate or large signal moves the parameter, before the confidence factor trims it by ×0.33, ×0.66 or ×1.00.

The two deltas are the only polled parameters, so they blend a measured poll with the analysts' drift. A fresh, Johor-specific poll dominates; the drift (capped at ±8 pp) only fills in when polling is stale or absent.

final_Δ = poll_confidence × poll + (1 − poll_confidence) × drift

Models in the shipped pipeline (from the call logs): GPT-5.5 for the judgment agents, the news extractor, the royal-feed reader, the poll search (with web search) and the briefing writer; GPT-4.1 for classifying party posts; GPT-4o for labelling comments; GPT-4o-mini for the cheap gates (is this post about politics? does this article mention Singapore politically?). Cheap models for high-volume yes/no work, the expensive one for judgement.

09 · BuildUpdating: the Daily Toast

The third interface was the simplest to describe and the most used. Twice a day, after the morning and evening update cycles, a model wrote a short situation report and pushed it out on Telegram. It was given two things: a digest of how the forecast had moved since the last update, with every number marked authoritative and never to be recomputed, and the new ground evidence the agents had read. Its instructions were to synthesise rather than enumerate, lead with the bottom line, and make the causal link explicit: the new evidence is why the forecast moved.

Here is a real one, from the evening of 7 July, the day the forecast dropped five seats in a single cycle.

🍞 Daily Toast · Johor PRN16
1. State of play

The model projected BN winning 38 of 56 seats, but 3 of those are inside the error band (5%), and a further 7 are won by under 10%. That still puts BN clearly above the 29-seat majority line, but the race is less locked than the headline seat count suggests because the opposition now has 11 narrow holds within 10 points of BN's reach, up from 6 this morning. Serom and Kota Iskandar are the tightest projected BN wins, so they should be treated as true toss-ups rather than leans. The broader campaign mood is mixed for BN: Malay comments toward BN warmed from 0.003 to 0.063 over the last five days, and mood toward the Johor government improved more sharply from −0.045 to 0.222. PH's Malay comment mood deteriorated from 0.175 to −0.029, which helps explain why BN still has a majority path despite today's seat losses. The Najib pardon issue is now a central risk because Nazifuddin Najib linked a big BN win in Kluang to support for Najib's release, and Anwar used Serom to frame the election as a vehicle for freeing Najib. BN leaders Hishammuddin Hussein and Azalina Othman Said are trying to separate the election from the pardon process. Opposition fragmentation still helps BN because PN is absent in 29 seats and Bersama is contesting 15, but PH's ground push is now reducing that advantage in several urban and marginal BN seats.

2. What moved today

BN's projection fell from 43 seats this morning to 38 seats tonight, still above the 29-seat majority line but with a materially thinner cushion. The main model driver was Malay support for BN being cut from 3.1 points above its 2022 level to only 0.53 points above 2022, which overwhelmed the unchanged Chinese BN support reading of −1.32 points versus 2022. Turnout did not drive the move because the target stayed at 56 and the Malay–Chinese turnout gap stayed at 20. Rural non-BN Malay alignment moved from 3 points toward PN versus 2022 to 2 points toward PN, which slightly helped PH where both opposition parties are actually on the ballot. The seat evidence was sharper than the statewide parameters: Tangkak, Layang-Layang, Endau, Tenggaroh and Tiram flipped from BN to the opposition column. Serom, Johor Jaya and Kota Iskandar slipped into BN toss-up territory. Rengit and Larkin are now only narrowly ahead for BN.

3. Singapore mentions

Anwar repeatedly drew a boundary around Singapore's role, saying Malaysia should not ask another country to interfere in its elections, even though companies in Singapore could be informed to ease voting arrangements for Malaysian workers. He also said Sunday voting would better suit Malaysians working half-days in Singapore, but stressed the Election Commission is independent. On the JS-SEZ, Anwar rejected claims that Johor alone controls the project, and Tengku Zafrul framed Singapore cooperation as a federal delivery story. Lim Kit Siang used Singapore to discuss overseas Malaysians and return migration.

10 · The machineWhat the final product looked like

34
days of live operation, 8 June to polling day
74
AI update cycles, each re-reading the evidence and re-setting the dials
25
dashboard versions shipped while it was running (build fast, fail cheaply)
56
seats re-forecast on every cycle

The dashboard had two faces. Monitoring showed the evidence, indicator by indicator, plus raw news and social feeds for anyone who wanted to read the source. Prediction showed the forecast: the seat count against the majority line, which seats were in play, the seat-by-seat table, and the AI reasoning panel explaining why the dials sat where they did. The sidebar held the manual override: an analyst could drag any dial, see the seats re-compute, and snap back to the AI's assessment with one click.

How the forecast moved over the campaign

Because every cycle was archived, we can replay the forecast. Drag the slider to any update and see the seat count and the six dials as they stood at that moment. The dashed line is the 29-seat majority; the marker on 1 July is nomination day, when the engine switched to modelling each seat's actual line-up.

—

Seat counts are what the dashboard displayed at the time, including the agents' per-seat overrides. Before 1 July every seat was modelled as a three-way contest; from 1 July on the real candidate list.

11 · Scoring the toastResults

The forecast was frozen at the close of polls on 11 July at BN 38 of 56, with 20 seats flagged as in play and five of BN's projected wins inside the engine's own error band. The yardstick we set ourselves in the Design phase was a 5% margin of error.
